medical.title: Routine invasive procedures for stable heart disease found to offer no long-term survival advantage over drug therapy
medical.summary: Patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who have invasive procedures early in their care do not live longer than those initially treated with drugs and lifestyle changes alone, an international study shows.

medical.title: AI used to predict cavities
medical.summary: An international team of researchers is leveraging artificial intelligence to predict who is at high risk for cavities. The findings, published in the journal Caries Research, could help identify population clusters most at risk for tooth decay based on larger social determinants of health rather than on clinical diagnostics at the individual level.

medical.title: Nearly 3 in 4 couples with unexplained infertility have a baby within two years of starting treatment
medical.summary: A new study has found nearly 3 out of 4 couples with unexplained infertility had a baby within two years of starting treatment, whether they received in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intrauterine insemination (IUI). While IVF led to faster pregnancies, long-term outcomes were similar for both treatments.

medical.title: After brain surgery, man sees cat's eyes in human faces
medical.summary: Karl, a 28-year-old man living in the northeastern United States, has a gray tabby cat named Luna. In the morning, his cat is often the first face that he sees.

medical.title: Over 9 million lives could be saved every year if countries met WHO air quality guidelines
medical.summary: Meeting the World Health Organization's recommended annual guidelines for air pollution resulting from fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide has the potential to save more than 9 million lives a year in low- and middle-income countries, say University of Cambridge researchers.

medical.title: Smoking linked to higher risk of dementia
medical.summary: A major review of more than 2 million people has found current smokers face a higher risk of dementia, with researchers calling for brain health to feature more prominently in antismoking campaigns.

medical.title: Nonprofit hospitals' financial assistance policies often don't reflect community need, study finds
medical.summary: Nonprofit hospitals in communities with the greatest financial needs offer eligibility for free care similar to that offered by hospitals in less disadvantaged communities, according to a new national study from Tulane University researchers. The study, published Nov. 2 in Health Affairs, analyzed 10 years of Internal Revenue Service data from more than 1,600 nonprofit hospitals.

medical.title: Cancer patients' voices could help improve care across Australia
medical.summary: Australians living with cancer are increasingly being asked a simple but powerful question: How are you? A study led by Flinders University and Flinders Medical Center describes how clinicians routinely listening to cancer patients about their symptoms, well-being and quality of life can transform cancer care.

medical.title: Singing in a choir may improve breathing and well-being in children born with a single heart ventricle
medical.summary: Singing in a choir strengthens breathing capacity, decreases depression and anxiety, and improves perceived school functioning in children born with a single heart ventricle, according to a feasibility study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in Pediatric Cardiology. This intervention, including in-person and online singing and breathing instruction, was developed and trialed in collaboration with Northwestern University Bienen School of Music.

medical.title: High lung pressure may protect newborns with diaphragmatic hernia from blood congestion
medical.summary: Brazilian research published in the journal Scientific Reports sheds light on the rapid and often fatal deterioration in the health of newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). In addition to uncovering the biological mechanism behind this sudden deterioration, the study raises concerns about the treatments currently used in neonatal intensive care units.

medical.title: New drug combination improves survival in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer
medical.summary: A new treatment approach could help people with an aggressive form of bladder cancer live longer and reduce the chances of their cancer returning or progressing, particularly those who cannot receive standard chemotherapy, according to findings from a large international clinical trial co-led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

medical.title: An inside look at a molecular switch that triggers inflammation
medical.summary: Researchers at VIB and Ghent University have uncovered how an important driver of inflammation is activated at the molecular level. Their findings, published in Science Immunology, also explain how a medicine used to treat a severe form of psoriasis blocks this inflammatory signal.

medical.title: Few meet major clinical response criteria after treatment escalation for lupus
medical.summary: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), fewer than one-quarter meet criteria for major clinical response (MCR) after treatment escalation, with Black patients less likely to meet MCR criteria than white patients, according to a study published online Nov. 2 in The Lancet Rheumatology.

medical.title: Scientists identify inhibition of a specific enzyme as a promising target to treat pancreatic cancer
medical.summary: Researchers have identified a promising new target in the treatment of pancreatic cancer. A new study in The American Journal of Pathology demonstrates that blocking complement factor B (CFB), a pivotal enzyme in the alternative complement pathway, halts cancer growth and alters the tumor microenvironment. The greatest tumor suppression was observed when CFB inhibition was combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

medical.title: Researchers reveal how inhaled nanoplastics trigger lung inflammation
medical.summary: Everyday plastic products, including water bottles, disposable cups and packaging, can break down over time into tiny fragments known as nanoplastics. These particles are invisible to the naked eye and can become airborne, raising concerns about their potential to reach deep into the lungs when inhaled.

medical.title: Could a flu shot help fight skin cancer?
medical.summary: Injecting an ordinary flu vaccine straight into skin cancer tumors may help rally the immune system against the cancer, a small early trial suggests.

medical.title: Expressive writing may help reduce negative alcohol-related consequences among people prone to heavy drinking
medical.summary: Writing about a drinking experience that went badly and associated feelings of guilt was linked to reduced negative alcohol-related consequences over the next year in a trial involving college students. Expressive writing may offer a fresh approach to brief alcohol interventions, which aim to motivate changes in drinking behaviors. It has been somewhat effective as a brief intervention for improving other aspects of well-being, such as emotional regulation and coping, though results for behavior change and heavy drinking have been mixed.

medical.title: Single-pill combination helps more patients control hypertension
medical.summary: Antihypertensive medications combined into a single pill lowered blood pressure more effectively than typical treatment with multiple pills for patients in Jamaica and Colombia, a study co-led by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers shows.

medical.title: FDA-approved drug kills cancer cells in lab by disrupting cellular recycling
medical.summary: Researchers from VCU Massey Comprehensive Cancer Center recently demonstrated that the inhibition of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) can cause death in cancer cells that is independent of changes in pro-death ceramide levels. The findings, which were recently published in Cell Death Discovery, showed that using eliglustat, an FDA-approved drug, induced cell death in several cancer cell lines. Additionally, the findings demonstrated, for the first time, that GCS and its products had a pro-survival role in cancer cells.

medical.title: Doxycycline use in early pregnancy associated with higher risk of pregnancy loss
medical.summary: A retrospective, active-comparator cohort study found that doxycycline use for respiratory tract infections or acne during early pregnancy was associated with an increased risk for pregnancy loss. Given the frequent use of doxycycline by women of childbearing age, these findings underscore the importance of both clinicians and patients weighing the benefits and risks when considering treatment with doxycycline. The findings are published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: New surface coating could help implants bond better with bone in people with diabetes
medical.summary: Flinders University researchers are launching an innovative surface-engineering technology that could help to raise the performance of implantable medical devices in people with diabetes and other metabolic diseases.

medical.title: Phone app alerts did not increase bystander CPR rates in study of two major population areas
medical.summary: A smartphone app designed to alert nearby CPR-trained volunteers resulted in similar response times for bystander CPR or automated external defibrillator (AED) use compared with the standard 911 response for people experiencing cardiac arrest, according to new, preliminary, independent late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium 2026 in Chicago.

medical.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

medical.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
medical.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

medical.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
medical.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

science.title: The surprising power of connecting with strangers
science.summary: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed.

science.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors.

science.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
science.summary: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates.

science.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
science.summary: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear.

science.title: Methane-eating microbes grown on electrodes build electrically conductive nanowires
science.summary: Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues published in Nature Communications now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab.

science.title: Cracking the case of the Roman frog graveyard
science.summary: Ten years after 8,000 ancient frog bones were discovered in a single ditch, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have finally identified the culprits

science.title: Water may play critical role in how our tissues stretch and spring back
science.summary: Every time your heart beats, your lungs expand, or your skin stretches, a remarkable protein called elastin helps your body return to its original shape. But what exactly gives this protein its elasticity? For more than 50 years, scientists have debated whether elastin's ability to stretch and recoil comes primarily from the protein's own flexibility or from its interactions with surrounding water molecules.

science.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
science.summary: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portray medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there's little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

science.title: Machine learning reveals how often fish schooling evolved—and repeatedly disappeared
science.summary: Scientists have used new machine learning techniques to investigate a topic no one has ever found a way to study: the evolution of fish moving together in schools across thousands of species. The new paper, published Nov. 6 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, is among the largest studies of the evolution of any behavior ever conducted in any group of species, according to the authors. The research shows that behaviors, which have previously been difficult to quantify, can be studied at a large evolutionary scale.

science.title: Tin deposits are formed from source rocks, not cooling
science.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has uncovered the primary drivers of tin mineralization, which will have significant implications for the discovery of tin deposits critical to the energy transition.

science.title: A parasite linked to cats may also threaten dogs' eyesight, researchers find
science.summary: A parasitic infection commonly associated with cats may be associated with severe, potentially sight-threatening ocular disease in dogs, according to a new study by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

science.title: Tree-rich landscapes help birds and bats nearly double cacao yields in Peru
science.summary: Tropical farmers are often expected to choose between high crop yields and protecting wildlife. However, an international team of researchers led by the University of Vienna, in collaboration with the universities of Göttingen and Würzburg in Germany and Bioversity International in Peru, shows that biodiversity conservation reinforces cacao production in agroforests via associated ecosystem services, such as natural pest control. The new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, provides important evidence for sustainable farm and landscape management in one of the world's most biodiverse regions.

science.title: The ELT can probe ultra-diffuse galaxies and their dark matter mysteries
science.summary: We've been waiting a long time for the Extremely Large Telescope's first light, scheduled for March 2029. Telescopes this large, powerful and costly always have multiple science goals, and that's true for the ELT. One of its science goals is to study fundamental aspects of the universe, including dark matter.

science.title: Did early humans collect keepsakes 500,000 years ago?
science.summary: Most of us are familiar with the urge to pick up a seashell from the beach or keep a stone from a hiking trip. The object itself may be ordinary, but to the person who keeps it, it serves as a reminder of a particular moment, place or person. Where did this behavior come from? Did early humans do the same? A new study by Tel Aviv University researchers suggests that this practice stretches back approximately half a million years, with important consequences for the evolution of memory.

science.title: Male lizard 'perfumes' may be more about rivalry than seduction
science.summary: Animals communicate in ways that are sometimes obvious to us and sometimes almost completely hidden. Bright colors, songs and courtship displays are easy to notice. Chemical signals are different: an animal can leave a message behind long after it has moved away.

science.title: A stellar odd couple at an unusual stage of evolution
science.summary: Most of the stars in the Milky Way are what we might call normal stars. They're main sequence stars like our sun, meaning they're doing what most people probably think stars do: shining as they fuse hydrogen atoms into helium atoms on a vast scale.

science.title: Upgraded microscope can now watch individual quantum particles in motion
science.summary: Energy can be carried in a number of ways: by electrons, the particles that underpin all modern electronics, as well as by quasiparticles, the results of different particles interacting with one another at the quantum level. Columbia chemist Milan Delor has been watching these different forms of energy flow with an instrument called stroboSCAT, a unique microscope that uses strobe-like light pulses to capture particles and quasiparticles as they move through different materials.

science.title: Rubies on Mars?
science.summary: Written by Roger C. Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University Nov. 4, 2026 Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected. Perseverance is equipped with a fantastic set of instruments for studying the rock record of this ancient planet. Both PIXL and SuperCam have great capabilities for detecting all kinds of […]

science.summary: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University Nov. 1, 2026 Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “Badger Peak.” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported, that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort […]

science.title: New perovskite system extends room-temperature spin polarization via successive quantum wells
science.summary: A research team led by Lu Haipeng, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), has achieved a breakthrough in preserving spin information for optoelectronic technologies. The team has developed a perovskite chiral multiple quantum-well system that maintains spin polarization approximately 300 times longer at room temperature. The study opens new possibilities for future quantum technologies and next-generation spin-based applications. The study was published in the journal Nature Photonics.

science.title: Computer science researcher reroutes truckloads of excess food from landfills to food pantries
science.summary: The planet already grows enough food to feed everyone. The problem is one of logistics. A third of all the food grown and raised goes to waste, meaning that one in 12 people does not have enough to eat.

science.title: Subaru Telescope reveals the shape and temperature of Comet Encke's nucleus
science.summary: Mid-infrared observations with the Subaru Telescope have revealed the shape and surface temperature of the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke. By analyzing how the nucleus's thermal emission changed as it rotated, the researchers found that the nucleus is elongated, with a long axis of about 7 kilometers and a short axis of about 3 kilometers. They also determined that the surface temperature at the time of observation was 328 ± 7 Kelvin (about 55°C).

science.title: Light reflecting within thin films can masquerade as molecular signals in perovskite solar materials
science.summary: An infrared signal thought to reveal how molecules in perovskite solar materials respond to light-generated charges can arise largely from the way light travels through the thin film itself, a new theoretical study shows. Jun Nishida, assistant professor at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), Japan, found that light-generated charges alter how infrared light is reflected and transmitted within the film layers, producing sharp features that resemble changes in molecular vibrations even when the vibrations themselves are unaltered.

science.title: New synthesis strategy controls handedness in large, light-emitting molecular spirals
science.summary: Helicenes are a class of organic molecules consisting of benzene rings arranged in a spiral-like shape. These molecules exhibit significant circularly polarized luminescence—emission of light with left or right handedness—and are expected to be utilized in 3D displays and anti-counterfeiting inks. Carbohelicenes, a subgroup of helicenes, are composed entirely of carbon and hydrogen.

science.title: Alternative approach could reduce reliance on potentially toxic surfactants in pharmaceutical and food applications
science.summary: An international research team led by the University of Sydney has found a way to formulate microemulsions without traditional surfactants, which are often toxic and hard to separate from end products. The findings have important implications for pharmaceutical applications and food additives.

environment.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
environment.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

environment.title: Money laundering complaints target JBS, Barclays over profits linked to illegal deforestation
environment.summary: A coalition of legal and environmental groups has filed money laundering complaints against JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, and 12 financial institutions, investors and advisers, including the U.K. bank Barclays. The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

environment.title: 3M agrees to pay more than $7 billion to settle ‘forever chemical’ groundwater contamination claims
environment.summary: Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products. The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people […]

environment.title: How Ghana’s new license to sell sustainable timber improves institutions & cooperation (analysis)
environment.summary: When Ghana began its Voluntary Partnership Agreement (VPA) process with the European Union, the attraction was clear. Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

environment.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

environment.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
environment.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

mix_items.title: The surprising power of connecting with strangers
mix_items.summary: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed.

mix_items.title: Routine invasive procedures for stable heart disease found to offer no long-term survival advantage over drug therapy
mix_items.summary: Patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who have invasive procedures early in their care do not live longer than those initially treated with drugs and lifestyle changes alone, an international study shows.

mix_items.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors.

mix_items.title: AI used to predict cavities
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers is leveraging artificial intelligence to predict who is at high risk for cavities. The findings, published in the journal Caries Research, could help identify population clusters most at risk for tooth decay based on larger social determinants of health rather than on clinical diagnostics at the individual level.

mix_items.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
mix_items.summary: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates.

mix_items.title: Nearly 3 in 4 couples with unexplained infertility have a baby within two years of starting treatment
mix_items.summary: A new study has found nearly 3 out of 4 couples with unexplained infertility had a baby within two years of starting treatment, whether they received in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intrauterine insemination (IUI). While IVF led to faster pregnancies, long-term outcomes were similar for both treatments.

mix_items.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
mix_items.summary: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear.

mix_items.title: Methane-eating microbes grown on electrodes build electrically conductive nanowires
mix_items.summary: Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues published in Nature Communications now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab.

mix_items.title: Cracking the case of the Roman frog graveyard
mix_items.summary: Ten years after 8,000 ancient frog bones were discovered in a single ditch, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have finally identified the culprits

mix_items.title: After brain surgery, man sees cat's eyes in human faces
mix_items.summary: Karl, a 28-year-old man living in the northeastern United States, has a gray tabby cat named Luna. In the morning, his cat is often the first face that he sees.

mix_items.title: Over 9 million lives could be saved every year if countries met WHO air quality guidelines
mix_items.summary: Meeting the World Health Organization's recommended annual guidelines for air pollution resulting from fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide has the potential to save more than 9 million lives a year in low- and middle-income countries, say University of Cambridge researchers.

mix_items.title: Smoking linked to higher risk of dementia
mix_items.summary: A major review of more than 2 million people has found current smokers face a higher risk of dementia, with researchers calling for brain health to feature more prominently in antismoking campaigns.

mix_items.title: Nonprofit hospitals' financial assistance policies often don't reflect community need, study finds
mix_items.summary: Nonprofit hospitals in communities with the greatest financial needs offer eligibility for free care similar to that offered by hospitals in less disadvantaged communities, according to a new national study from Tulane University researchers. The study, published Nov. 2 in Health Affairs, analyzed 10 years of Internal Revenue Service data from more than 1,600 nonprofit hospitals.

mix_items.title: Water may play critical role in how our tissues stretch and spring back
mix_items.summary: Every time your heart beats, your lungs expand, or your skin stretches, a remarkable protein called elastin helps your body return to its original shape. But what exactly gives this protein its elasticity? For more than 50 years, scientists have debated whether elastin's ability to stretch and recoil comes primarily from the protein's own flexibility or from its interactions with surrounding water molecules.

mix_items.title: Cancer patients' voices could help improve care across Australia
mix_items.summary: Australians living with cancer are increasingly being asked a simple but powerful question: How are you? A study led by Flinders University and Flinders Medical Center describes how clinicians routinely listening to cancer patients about their symptoms, well-being and quality of life can transform cancer care.

mix_items.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
mix_items.summary: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portray medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there's little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

mix_items.title: Singing in a choir may improve breathing and well-being in children born with a single heart ventricle
mix_items.summary: Singing in a choir strengthens breathing capacity, decreases depression and anxiety, and improves perceived school functioning in children born with a single heart ventricle, according to a feasibility study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in Pediatric Cardiology. This intervention, including in-person and online singing and breathing instruction, was developed and trialed in collaboration with Northwestern University Bienen School of Music.

mix_items.title: High lung pressure may protect newborns with diaphragmatic hernia from blood congestion
mix_items.summary: Brazilian research published in the journal Scientific Reports sheds light on the rapid and often fatal deterioration in the health of newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). In addition to uncovering the biological mechanism behind this sudden deterioration, the study raises concerns about the treatments currently used in neonatal intensive care units.

mix_items.title: Machine learning reveals how often fish schooling evolved—and repeatedly disappeared
mix_items.summary: Scientists have used new machine learning techniques to investigate a topic no one has ever found a way to study: the evolution of fish moving together in schools across thousands of species. The new paper, published Nov. 6 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, is among the largest studies of the evolution of any behavior ever conducted in any group of species, according to the authors. The research shows that behaviors, which have previously been difficult to quantify, can be studied at a large evolutionary scale.

mix_items.title: New drug combination improves survival in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer
mix_items.summary: A new treatment approach could help people with an aggressive form of bladder cancer live longer and reduce the chances of their cancer returning or progressing, particularly those who cannot receive standard chemotherapy, according to findings from a large international clinical trial co-led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Tin deposits are formed from source rocks, not cooling
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has uncovered the primary drivers of tin mineralization, which will have significant implications for the discovery of tin deposits critical to the energy transition.

mix_items.title: A parasite linked to cats may also threaten dogs' eyesight, researchers find
mix_items.summary: A parasitic infection commonly associated with cats may be associated with severe, potentially sight-threatening ocular disease in dogs, according to a new study by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

mix_items.title: An inside look at a molecular switch that triggers inflammation
mix_items.summary: Researchers at VIB and Ghent University have uncovered how an important driver of inflammation is activated at the molecular level. Their findings, published in Science Immunology, also explain how a medicine used to treat a severe form of psoriasis blocks this inflammatory signal.

mix_items.title: Few meet major clinical response criteria after treatment escalation for lupus
mix_items.summary: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), fewer than one-quarter meet criteria for major clinical response (MCR) after treatment escalation, with Black patients less likely to meet MCR criteria than white patients, according to a study published online Nov. 2 in The Lancet Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: Tree-rich landscapes help birds and bats nearly double cacao yields in Peru
mix_items.summary: Tropical farmers are often expected to choose between high crop yields and protecting wildlife. However, an international team of researchers led by the University of Vienna, in collaboration with the universities of Göttingen and Würzburg in Germany and Bioversity International in Peru, shows that biodiversity conservation reinforces cacao production in agroforests via associated ecosystem services, such as natural pest control. The new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, provides important evidence for sustainable farm and landscape management in one of the world's most biodiverse regions.

mix_items.title: The ELT can probe ultra-diffuse galaxies and their dark matter mysteries
mix_items.summary: We've been waiting a long time for the Extremely Large Telescope's first light, scheduled for March 2029. Telescopes this large, powerful and costly always have multiple science goals, and that's true for the ELT. One of its science goals is to study fundamental aspects of the universe, including dark matter.

mix_items.title: Scientists identify inhibition of a specific enzyme as a promising target to treat pancreatic cancer
mix_items.summary: Researchers have identified a promising new target in the treatment of pancreatic cancer. A new study in The American Journal of Pathology demonstrates that blocking complement factor B (CFB), a pivotal enzyme in the alternative complement pathway, halts cancer growth and alters the tumor microenvironment. The greatest tumor suppression was observed when CFB inhibition was combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: Did early humans collect keepsakes 500,000 years ago?
mix_items.summary: Most of us are familiar with the urge to pick up a seashell from the beach or keep a stone from a hiking trip. The object itself may be ordinary, but to the person who keeps it, it serves as a reminder of a particular moment, place or person. Where did this behavior come from? Did early humans do the same? A new study by Tel Aviv University researchers suggests that this practice stretches back approximately half a million years, with important consequences for the evolution of memory.

mix_items.title: Researchers reveal how inhaled nanoplastics trigger lung inflammation
mix_items.summary: Everyday plastic products, including water bottles, disposable cups and packaging, can break down over time into tiny fragments known as nanoplastics. These particles are invisible to the naked eye and can become airborne, raising concerns about their potential to reach deep into the lungs when inhaled.

mix_items.title: Male lizard 'perfumes' may be more about rivalry than seduction
mix_items.summary: Animals communicate in ways that are sometimes obvious to us and sometimes almost completely hidden. Bright colors, songs and courtship displays are easy to notice. Chemical signals are different: an animal can leave a message behind long after it has moved away.

mix_items.title: A stellar odd couple at an unusual stage of evolution
mix_items.summary: Most of the stars in the Milky Way are what we might call normal stars. They're main sequence stars like our sun, meaning they're doing what most people probably think stars do: shining as they fuse hydrogen atoms into helium atoms on a vast scale.

mix_items.title: Could a flu shot help fight skin cancer?
mix_items.summary: Injecting an ordinary flu vaccine straight into skin cancer tumors may help rally the immune system against the cancer, a small early trial suggests.

mix_items.title: Upgraded microscope can now watch individual quantum particles in motion
mix_items.summary: Energy can be carried in a number of ways: by electrons, the particles that underpin all modern electronics, as well as by quasiparticles, the results of different particles interacting with one another at the quantum level. Columbia chemist Milan Delor has been watching these different forms of energy flow with an instrument called stroboSCAT, a unique microscope that uses strobe-like light pulses to capture particles and quasiparticles as they move through different materials.

mix_items.title: Expressive writing may help reduce negative alcohol-related consequences among people prone to heavy drinking
mix_items.summary: Writing about a drinking experience that went badly and associated feelings of guilt was linked to reduced negative alcohol-related consequences over the next year in a trial involving college students. Expressive writing may offer a fresh approach to brief alcohol interventions, which aim to motivate changes in drinking behaviors. It has been somewhat effective as a brief intervention for improving other aspects of well-being, such as emotional regulation and coping, though results for behavior change and heavy drinking have been mixed.

mix_items.title: Rubies on Mars?
mix_items.summary: Written by Roger C. Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University Nov. 4, 2026 Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected. Perseverance is equipped with a fantastic set of instruments for studying the rock record of this ancient planet. Both PIXL and SuperCam have great capabilities for detecting all kinds of […]

mix_items.title: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?
mix_items.summary: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University Nov. 1, 2026 Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “Badger Peak.” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported, that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort […]

mix_items.title: New perovskite system extends room-temperature spin polarization via successive quantum wells
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Lu Haipeng, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), has achieved a breakthrough in preserving spin information for optoelectronic technologies. The team has developed a perovskite chiral multiple quantum-well system that maintains spin polarization approximately 300 times longer at room temperature. The study opens new possibilities for future quantum technologies and next-generation spin-based applications. The study was published in the journal Nature Photonics.

mix_items.title: Single-pill combination helps more patients control hypertension
mix_items.summary: Antihypertensive medications combined into a single pill lowered blood pressure more effectively than typical treatment with multiple pills for patients in Jamaica and Colombia, a study co-led by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers shows.

mix_items.title: Computer science researcher reroutes truckloads of excess food from landfills to food pantries
mix_items.summary: The planet already grows enough food to feed everyone. The problem is one of logistics. A third of all the food grown and raised goes to waste, meaning that one in 12 people does not have enough to eat.

mix_items.title: Subaru Telescope reveals the shape and temperature of Comet Encke's nucleus
mix_items.summary: Mid-infrared observations with the Subaru Telescope have revealed the shape and surface temperature of the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke. By analyzing how the nucleus's thermal emission changed as it rotated, the researchers found that the nucleus is elongated, with a long axis of about 7 kilometers and a short axis of about 3 kilometers. They also determined that the surface temperature at the time of observation was 328 ± 7 Kelvin (about 55°C).

mix_items.title: FDA-approved drug kills cancer cells in lab by disrupting cellular recycling
mix_items.summary: Researchers from VCU Massey Comprehensive Cancer Center recently demonstrated that the inhibition of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) can cause death in cancer cells that is independent of changes in pro-death ceramide levels. The findings, which were recently published in Cell Death Discovery, showed that using eliglustat, an FDA-approved drug, induced cell death in several cancer cell lines. Additionally, the findings demonstrated, for the first time, that GCS and its products had a pro-survival role in cancer cells.

mix_items.title: Light reflecting within thin films can masquerade as molecular signals in perovskite solar materials
mix_items.summary: An infrared signal thought to reveal how molecules in perovskite solar materials respond to light-generated charges can arise largely from the way light travels through the thin film itself, a new theoretical study shows. Jun Nishida, assistant professor at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), Japan, found that light-generated charges alter how infrared light is reflected and transmitted within the film layers, producing sharp features that resemble changes in molecular vibrations even when the vibrations themselves are unaltered.

mix_items.title: Doxycycline use in early pregnancy associated with higher risk of pregnancy loss
mix_items.summary: A retrospective, active-comparator cohort study found that doxycycline use for respiratory tract infections or acne during early pregnancy was associated with an increased risk for pregnancy loss. Given the frequent use of doxycycline by women of childbearing age, these findings underscore the importance of both clinicians and patients weighing the benefits and risks when considering treatment with doxycycline. The findings are published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: New synthesis strategy controls handedness in large, light-emitting molecular spirals
mix_items.summary: Helicenes are a class of organic molecules consisting of benzene rings arranged in a spiral-like shape. These molecules exhibit significant circularly polarized luminescence—emission of light with left or right handedness—and are expected to be utilized in 3D displays and anti-counterfeiting inks. Carbohelicenes, a subgroup of helicenes, are composed entirely of carbon and hydrogen.

mix_items.title: New surface coating could help implants bond better with bone in people with diabetes
mix_items.summary: Flinders University researchers are launching an innovative surface-engineering technology that could help to raise the performance of implantable medical devices in people with diabetes and other metabolic diseases.

mix_items.title: Alternative approach could reduce reliance on potentially toxic surfactants in pharmaceutical and food applications
mix_items.summary: An international research team led by the University of Sydney has found a way to formulate microemulsions without traditional surfactants, which are often toxic and hard to separate from end products. The findings have important implications for pharmaceutical applications and food additives.

mix_items.title: Phone app alerts did not increase bystander CPR rates in study of two major population areas
mix_items.summary: A smartphone app designed to alert nearby CPR-trained volunteers resulted in similar response times for bystander CPR or automated external defibrillator (AED) use compared with the standard 911 response for people experiencing cardiac arrest, according to new, preliminary, independent late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium 2026 in Chicago.

mix_items.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
mix_items.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

mix_items.title: Money laundering complaints target JBS, Barclays over profits linked to illegal deforestation
mix_items.summary: A coalition of legal and environmental groups has filed money laundering complaints against JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, and 12 financial institutions, investors and advisers, including the U.K. bank Barclays. The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

mix_items.title: 3M agrees to pay more than $7 billion to settle ‘forever chemical’ groundwater contamination claims
mix_items.summary: Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products. The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people […]

mix_items.title: How Ghana’s new license to sell sustainable timber improves institutions & cooperation (analysis)
mix_items.summary: When Ghana began its Voluntary Partnership Agreement (VPA) process with the European Union, the attraction was clear. Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

mix_items.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

mix_items.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
mix_items.summary: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

mix_items.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
mix_items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

mix_items.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
mix_items.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.
